route.basis: The generic target names the English-taught International Business Communication specialisation. The adopted OER offers English and optional Spanish language tracks; English is the broad default without an added Spanish-language requirement. The three thematic profiles are possible academic directions, not a reason to replace the formal English-track curriculum or prefill 30 EC of minor and 30 EC of free electives.

modules.title: Introduction to CIS
modules.aims: By the end of the course, you can: describe how meaning, identity, and relationships are formed through communication describe the relationship between culture and communication explain how context and medium influence the goals and form of communication distinguish different approaches to research in the field of CIS

modules.title: Language, Communication, and Media
modules.assessment: The course will be graded based on an individual portfolio consisting of different assignments (pass/fail), and a final exam (digital testing via ANS), about the lectures and the course literature (minimal passing grade: 5.5).
modules.aims: Upon successful completion of this course you can : explain central concepts and theoretical approaches in the study of language use in media; distinguish the significance of specific examples of language use in media; apply central concepts from language use in mediated communication to real-world examples; make initial analyses of language use in (mass) mediated communication.

modules.title: Digital Communication
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students can: Explain and illustrate key concepts and terminology related to digital communication using relevant examples. Apply multiple methodological approaches and concepts to study digital communication in various contexts. Identify and explain similarities and differences of language use across different digital media platforms. Analyze the relationship between media characteristics and interactional patterns in digital communication. Examine and reflect on the interactional and contextual implications of how people use language in digital environments. Assess insights from the course for relevance within a chosen context, creatively apply these insights by translating them into a digital product, and clearly present this product to an audience of peers.

modules.title: Social Interaction
modules.aims: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: 1. handle and apply the main concepts and their meanings from the field of interaction analysis; 2. select and transcribe a conversational excerpt according to current conventions; 3. analyze conversation excerpts for interactional aspects such as turn-taking, sequential organization and repair; 4. link a data-driven analysis to previous interaction research in an oral presentation.

modules.title: Corporate Communication
modules.entry: Note for exchange students: you cannot take this course if your English proficiency level is not at least B2 (TOEFL, IELTS, TOEIC or Cambridge). A statement from your home university won't be accepted.
modules.assessment: Note for international students: this course includes an on-campus exam in January that you cannot take remotely. The resit exam at the end of March or beginning of April can also not be taken remotely.
modules.aims: At the end of this course, a student can: Identify the most important elements of corporate communication and describe interrelationships between these elements; Distinguish the corporate communication goals of organisations and recognise the strategies organisations use to attain these goals; Understand and apply the most important insights of different specialist areas of corporate communication; Analyse actual cases of corporate communication and give informed evaluations of the success of this communication.

modules.title: Research Orientation and Academic Skills
modules.aims: This course provides an important foundation for student success in the overall BA programme, as it focuses on essential skills for studying at a university and functioning in an academic context. Such skills relate to reflecting on suitable approaches to research in Communication and Information Studies, critical reading and reasoning, effective academic writing, and constructive collaboration. The course aims to achieve the following learning objectives: Research orientation: students can identify and explain different research questions and strategies, research methodologies (e.g. qualitative and quantitative), and data types; Academic reading: students can search for, select, critically read, summarize and assess academic literature starting from a set research topic; Academic topic choice: students can determine a specific research focus on a set research topic and articulate its relevance for theory and practice, based on relevant academic sources; Academic writing: students can individually write a concise Introduction section to a research proposal (including a theoretical framework) leading to a relevant research question; Academic writing: students can individually write clear, coherent, and logically structured texts, using an academic writing style, in accordance with the academic conventions (e.g., APA referencing); Academic (peer) reviewing: students can assess their own and others’ academic writing and provide constructive feedback.

modules.title: Intercultural Communication
modules.entry: Note for exchange students: you cannot take this course if your English proficiency level is not at least B2 (TOEFL, IELTS, TOEIC or Cambridge). A statement from your home university won't be accepted.
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students will: Be able to identify and describe fundamental theoretical concepts and principles that are relevant to understanding communication between people from different cultural and social backgrounds; Have insight into the concept of culture, cultural differences and how culture can influence verbal and non-verbal behaviour; Have insight into contributors to - and issues in - intercultural communication, and be able to reflect critically on these; Have insight into acculturation/cultural adaptation, culture shock, and the development of intercultural communication competence, and be able to identify and critically reflect on factors that play a role in these processes.

modules.title: Communication and Persuasion
modules.entry: Note for exchange students: you cannot take this course if your English proficiency level is not at least B2 (TOEFL, IELTS, TOEIC or Cambridge). A statement from your home university won't be accepted. This course covers the basics of persuasive communication and requires no prior knowledge or skills in this particular field.
modules.aims: At the end of the course students: 1. have knowledge of the main theories in the field of persuasive communication 2. are able to recognize and name the central concepts from these theories 3. know which textual, linguistic, and visual elements play a role in the persuasion process 4. are able to analyze and critically evaluate practical examples of persuasive communication 5. can develop a persuasive message of which the design choices are informed by theoretical knowledge about the processing and effects of persuasive communication.

modules.title: Communication and Understanding
modules.aims: At the end of this course, you can: describe how people construct situation models on the basis of communicative input explain how features of the discourse and of the reader/listener influence comprehension analyse the coherence, cohesion, and information structure of a discourse create an explanatory text that is optimized for understanding by a particular audience, and motivate your text design choices orally present an explanation of a complex topic

modules.title: Information Science
modules.entry: Note for exchange students: you cannot take this course if your English proficiency level is not at least B2 (TOEFL, IELTS, TOEIC or Cambridge). A statement from your home university won't be accepted.
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students will be able to: Describe how people create, process and communicate data, information and knowledge, and apply this knowledge for tasks in your academic and personal life. Explain how computers process data and information and how those are shared on the Internet. Appraise the opportunities and risks of generative AI tools and digital technologies in general for our society. Use the knowledge from learning goals 1,2 and 3 to critically evaluate and manage your information behaviour, including your digital footprint. Investigate existing literature on a topic of the course and represent your findings in the form of a visually effective presentation, created with the help of digital tools.

modules.title: Marketing Communication
modules.entry: Note for exchange students: you cannot take this course if your English proficiency level is not at least B2 (TOEFL, IELTS, TOEIC or Cambridge). A statement from your home university won't be accepted. This course covers the basics of marketing communication and requires no prior knowledge or skills in the marketing field.
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students can: Recognize and explain the role of communication in different marketing processes Name, explain, identify, and relate the principal forms and strategies in marketing communication Name and explain relevant theories, models, and research findings about the impact of marketing communication on consumer cognition, attitudes and behaviour Apply their knowledge about the topics above to design and substantiate a marketing communication plan Apply their knowledge about the topics above to analyse and critically reflect on marketing communication activities

modules.title: Data Description and Visualisation
modules.aims: The goal of this course is to develop students' basic understanding and skills related to the research process and descriptive statistics, with a particular focus on survey research. By the conclusion of this course, students will be able to: understand the basics of the research process; understand the basics of descriptive statistics; understand the important aspects of conducting survey research; describe, visualize and interpret data (from survey research); carry out a survey research project in groups (with support from the instructor) and to write a research report about the results

modules.title: Interaction and Discourse Analysis
modules.aims: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: Explain the essence of interaction analysis and discourse analysis based on relevant theoretical concepts; Develop a (critical) perspective for systematic qualitative analysis of data; Analyze the communicative function of verbal (and visual) features within the broader context (social, political, cultural) in which the text is produced and used, with a focus on critical discourse analysis, cultural discourse analysis and framing analysis; Analyze social communication and interaction following appropriate qualitative methods, particularly ethnomethodology, ethnography and fieldwork-based methods.

modules.title: Experimental Research in Business Communication
modules.aims: The aim of the course is to acquire knowledge and skills that are crucial for designing and conducting experimental research. Upon completion of the course, the student has: knowledge of aspects that are important when designing an experiment and is able to apply this knowledge in their own research (exam); knowledge of statistical analyses that are commonly used in experimental research and can interpret the output of these analyses (exam); the skills to appropriately analyse data obtained from experimental research (assignment); the skills to design and conduct experimental research in a group setting and to report on this (assignment).

modules.title: Language in International Business
modules.aims: By the end of the course, students can: Explain the theoretical frameworks that describe the role of language areas of identity, team work, and power in international business Analyse how language proficiency affects employees in international business contexts Apply their theoretical knowledge to critically examine a real-life business case, identifying how language dynamics show up in a real-life business case Reflect on the relationship between theory and practice by evaluating how well academics theories are able to account for real-world business situations

modules.title: Philosophy of Communication
modules.aims: At the end of the course the student will be able to: Apply and explain important philosophical concepts that are relevant to the study of communication. Read and critically evaluate philosophical texts on a basic level. Provide an ethical analysis of case studies of relevance within the field of communication.

modules.title: Cross-Cultural Online Communication
modules.entry: Attention: A basic knowledge of statistics and SPSS. To participate in Cross-Cultural Language Use Spanish, students must have obtained at least 10 of the 15 ECTS of Spanish-language courses from the B2 (i.e., 2 of the 3 subjects).
modules.assessment: Examination: - Written examination based on information covered in the primary literature and lectures (after period 1) (40%) - Final paper about the collective contrastive corpus compiled for the target language. The introduction to this paper will be provided by the lecturers. Assessment will only take place on the basis of the following sections in the report: Research Question, Methodology, Results and Conclusion & Discussion. (60%) Participation in the lectures is not compulsory, but participation in the seminars is compulsory. If a student attends less than 65% of the seminars in period 2, they will be excluded from both the first and second opportunity to take the examination for this part of the course (= final paper). The student shall then be unable to complete the course in the relevant academic year. (EER): “A student who is absent from more than 35% of the lectures of a course in one period is excluded from further participation in the course and from the partial and interim examinations that are part of the course.” (see https://tinyurl.com/bdhhmkny ) Final papers must be uploaded via BRIGHTSPACE and, if requested by the lecturer, must also be submitted as hard copies. The hand-in time shown on BRIGHTSPACE will be used to determine whether the deadline was met. Students caught engaging in plagiarism will be reported to the Examining Board which will handle this issue (see https://www.ru.nl/facultyofarts/stip/rules-guidelines/education-assessment/fraud-plagiarism). If a student scores less than a 5.5 on the written examination or the research article, they must take the resit. If the course is not completed with a passing grade, the student must take the entire course again (partial grades will expire).
modules.aims: 1. Learning objectives At the end of this course, the student will be able to reflect critically on primary literature in the area of intercultural communication, will have mastered the basic principles of setting up corpus research, will have learned to develop and test an analysis model and will have reported in the target language of a contrasting corpus analysis. Regarding the written examination, the student will demonstrate that they: Can explain and motivate the choice of literature Can reflect critically on the primary literature Can link the models used in the literature Can apply the analysis models used in the literature to new material With regard to the paper, in the form of a scientific article, the student demonstrates that they are able to: Accurately describe the method used Analyse and report the results In the conclusion/discussion section, place his/her results in the context of the research and scientific field and reflect on, as well as translate, the consequences of the research to the professional field Report scientifically in the target language on his/her research

modules.title: Global English
modules.aims: At the end of the course students are able to: describe the main factors in the spread of English globally and how varieties of English have evolved. describe the various professional and informal communication contexts in which English is used, and how it has impacted culture, media, societies, various types of organizations, teams and individuals. analyze and reflect on effects of global English (use) from an individual language user's perspective on aspects such as identity formation, professional performance, well-being, linguistic exclusion, and discrimination. reflect on contrasting perspectives held by researchers on global English as a phenomenon. understand the general academic and societal relevance of knowledge on English as a global language. explain, summarize and discuss specialized course content to peers and general audiences in spoken and written contexts.

modules.title: Personal and Professional Development
modules.aims: Na afloop van deze B3 PPO cursus kun je als student: 1) een persoonlijk portfolio waarin je je ontwikkeling zichtbaar maakt, opbouwen en onderhouden. 2) je eigen verhaal vormgeven: je eigen profiel ontwikkelen, verbanden leggen tussen je studie en je toekomstmogelijkheden en een eindreflectie schrijven op je leerproces, vaardigheden en loopbaanoriëntatie. 3) inzichten en oplossingen bieden voor een maatschappelijk vraagstuk door jouw kennis en vaardigheden in te zetten in een (onderzoeks)project; 4) in teamverband een projectplan opstellen voor een (onderzoeks)project, waarin je het project definieert en afbakent en de projectactiviteiten beschrijft en plant; 5) in teamverband de projectactiviteiten verdelen en uitvoeren en hierbij constructief samenwerken, rekening houdend met de verschillende belangen van de betrokken partijen; 6) de resultaten van het (onderzoeks)project op een heldere en voor de betrokken partijen relevante manier presenteren; 7) reflecteren op je eigen kwaliteiten en op de ontwikkeling die je hebt doorgemaakt bij het werken in een team en het uitvoeren van het project.

modules.title: Cross-cultural language use English
modules.entry: A basic knowledge of statistics and SPSS is required.
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students: - are able to critically assess academic literature in the field of non-nativeness in English in international business communication - can apply their knowledge of non-nativeness in analysing and reporting an experimental study into the effect of an aspect of non-nativeness in English on the recipient of a message - can analyse the results of this study and report in English at C1 level.

modules.title: Academic and Professional Language Skills English
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students can: - communicate in English when writing about subjects relevant to international business communication (e.g. crisis communication, 'startups', social media policy) - in a series of individual writing assignments in academic and professional contexts (e.g. management reports, social media case analysis, crisis communication advice, editorial, press release) - at CEFR level C1/C2.

modules.title: Bachelor's thesis
modules.entry: Bachelor students IBC are only allowed to start with the thesis at the beginning of the second semester of the third bachelor year.
modules.aims: At the end of the course, students will be capable of: • Finding, understanding and using relevant literature with the aim of formulating and substantiating a research question; • Setting up a useful, feasible, valid and reliable research study to answer the research question; • Answering a research question by analysing and interpreting the data obtained; • Linking the research results to the existing literature and the professional field; • Reporting on these results in the form of an academic paper.

modules.title: Mentorship IBC
modules.assessment: Test information During your whole bachelor’s you will work on your personal and professional development (PPD) and you will record this development in a portfolio (Portflow). You will not be graded at the end of the Mentoring program, but instead the end result is a ‘pass’ or ‘no pass’. Successfully ending your mentoring program is your first milestone in the PPD learning trajectory. The time you spend on PPD and building up your portfolio, including the time you invest during this mentoring program, will be rewarded in a course in the last/third year of your bachelor’s.
modules.aims: Aims At the end of the course, the student is able to reflect on their personal and professional development and shape this development by identifying and substantiating their own needs and insights and by making informed choices. by engaging in activities to the benefit of their own development in the program (and for the benefit of their future career)

modules.title: Mentorship and PPO IBC B2

The time you spend on PPD and building up your portfolio, including the time you invest during this mentoring program, will be rewarded in a course in the last/third year of your bachelor’s.

governingRules.programme: Article 5 English B1 and B2 and shared IBC B3, pp. 8, 10 and 11. 60+60+60 EC including separate 30 EC choice allocations. Article 10 establishes IBC thesis start and the Spanish module prerequisite. Article 6 is the study-abroad substitution case.
governingRules.faculty: Article 10 pp. 8–9 requires two fixed 15 EC Faculty of Arts minors for the 2026 cohort. Free space is broadening bachelor study outside the own programme. Foreign courses require advance approval.
governingRules.participation: Zero-credit mentorship and portfolio work, RADAr and seminar attendance. Examiner exception applies to absence rule. Practical assignments can condition exams. Exchange-only B2 English requirements in module records are distinct from entry to the regular route.
governingRules.language: Module 204 presumes statistics and SPSS. Its Spanish credit sentence expressly names Cross-Cultural Language Use Spanish. The English language use module also requires statistics/SPSS. Thesis starts in semester two under the OER and current module entry. Prospective 2027–2030 tables are contextual.
